annotations.tweet_text: We accommodate every faith's dietary rules in schools now. At some point you have to ask whose schools these are.
annotations.participant_label: Ambiguous -- could be read as harmful or legitimate depending on who is reading and why
annotations.rationale: I think this might be seen as harmful because it's talking about schools and kids. Schools should be places where every child feels included, and statements like this can make it sound like some students don't really belong because of their religion. I think that if you have special dietary requirements for religious reasons, it's mostly your or your parents' responsibility to make sure those needs are met. But at the same time, schools should also be practical. If, for example, 20% or more of the students are Muslim and can't eat pork, it seems reasonable to offer another meal option. That doesn't force anything on anyone—it just gives those kids something they can eat while everyone else can still choose what they want. Religion is your choice and you must take responsibility  for your kids and what they eat without obligation school or goverment.

annotations.tweet_text: I have no problem with people praying five times a day. I do have a problem when it starts affecting workplace schedules for everyone else.
annotations.participant_label: Ambiguous -- could be read as harmful or legitimate depending on who is reading and why
annotations.rationale: It could be harmful for Muslim people who pray five times a day. Once again, if you made the decision to be Muslim and pray five times a day, it is your choice, but you must also be respectful of your environment. Be considerate and do it in a private place. If you need to pray during working hours, make sure it does not interrupt anybody, and the time you spend praying should not be paid for by the employer. Even if it may seem harmful to religious people, I think it is a reasonable statement.

annotations.tweet_text: There's a reason the Enlightenment happened in one part of the world and not others. That's not racism, it's history.
annotations.participant_label: Not harmful -- policy concern, cultural commentary, or frustration with no hateful subtext
annotations.participant_target: Immigrants, refugees, or a racialised group
annotations.rationale: For me this statement is not harmful. I think it is important to acknowledge history, even when it discusses differences between regions or societies. Historical events happen for many different reasons, including cultural, political, economic, and social factors, and understanding those connections helps us learn from the past. Saying that there are historical reasons why the Enlightenment began in one part of the world is not, by itself, an attack on any race or religion. As long as the discussion is based on historical evidence and not used to stereotype or discriminate against people today, I believe it is a reasonable statement rather than a harmful one.

annotations.tweet_text: Female genital mutilation is illegal here. Calling attention to where it's practiced is not Islamophobia.
annotations.participant_label: Not harmful -- policy concern, cultural commentary, or frustration with no hateful subtext
annotations.rationale: I agree with this statement. Female genital mutilation is illegal, and I think it's important to talk openly about where it is still practiced. The focus should be on protecting girls and women, not on avoiding the topic because it might offend someone. Criticizing a practice is different from criticizing an entire religion or all of its followers.
